items.note: Used any time before roughly late morning; casual speech drops ございます (gozaimasu) to just おはよう (ohayō) among friends and family.
The generic daytime greeting, used from around late morning through the afternoon; it can also serve as a general 'hello', e.g. when visiting someone.
Used once it starts getting dark, roughly evening onward — the evening counterpart to こんにちは (konnichiwa).
A more formal or definitive goodbye than じゃあまた (jaa mata); it can suggest you won't see the person again soon, so it's less used for everyday partings.
A casual goodbye for someone you expect to see again soon; さようなら (sayōnara) is more formal and can sound more final.
Covers apology, 'excuse me' to get someone's attention, and even a casual thank-you for trouble taken — the meaning shifts with context.
Used only at the very start of meeting someone for the first time; よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu) usually follows to close the introduction.

items.target: よろしくおねがいします
items.note: Said right after はじめまして (hajimemashite) to close a first introduction; roughly 'please treat me well going forward', with no direct English equivalent.
items.scene: said at the end of an introduction

items.note: -じん (jin) attached to a country name means 'person from there'; フランス (furansu) alone is just the country.
-じん (jin) attached to a country name means 'person from there'; ちゅうごく (chūgoku) alone is just the country.
-じん (jin) attached to a country name means 'person from there'; かんこく (kankoku) alone is just the country.
-じん (jin) attached to a country name means 'person from there'; イギリス (igirisu) alone is just the country.
Also covers 'I don't understand'; it's the negative form of わかります (wakarimasu, 'to understand/know').

items.target: ジャックさんはフランスじんですか？
ライアンさんはイギリスじんですか？
こちらはイギリスのライアンです
items.note: Here の (no) links country and name ('Ryan of England'); contrast with -じん (jin), which turns the country itself into a nationality noun, as in イギリスじん (igirisu jin).

items.target: しゅっしんはどこですか？
items.note: Asks generally where someone is from (hometown/origin) — an open-ended alternative to directly guessing nationality with ~さんは[country]じんですか, like ジャックさんはフランスじんですか (Jakku san wa furansu jin desu ka?) in this lesson.

items.english: Nice to meet you, my name is Ryan
items.target: はじめまして。ライアンです
わたしはイギリスじんです

items.note: The occupation noun for doctor; when addressing or talking about a doctor directly, use せんせい (sensei) instead, just as with teachers.
Also used directly as a title of address for teachers, doctors, and other professionals (e.g. saying 先生 to or about them instead of their name), not just as the occupation noun.

がくせい (gakusei) is only the occupation/category noun for 'student'; unlike せんせい (sensei) 'teacher' from this lesson, it's never used as a term of direct address — you'd address a student by name + さん (san), not がくせいさん.
Uses なん (nan), the form なに (nani) takes before です (desu) and many counters/particles.

items.english: What is James's mobile phone number?
items.target: ジェームズさんのけいたいばんごうはなんですか
items.note: Uses なん (nan), the form なに (nani) takes before です (desu) — the same pattern explained under なんですか (nan desu ka) earlier in this lesson.

items.target: わたしのけいたいばんごうは[number]です

items.note: Uses の (no) to link to an owner, e.g. ホテルのじゅうしょ (hoteru no jūsho, 'the hotel's address') or わたしのじゅうしょ (watashi no jūsho, 'my address') — the same の pattern as こちらはイギリスのライアンです (kochira wa igirisu no raian desu).

items.target: ホテルのじゅうしょはどこですか
わたしのじゅうしょは
ホテルのじゅうしょは

items.note: いくら (ikura) is the question word for price/amount specifically; contrast なん (nan) 'what' (なんですか, nan desu ka) and どこ (doko) 'where' (as in しゅっしんはどこですか, shusshin wa doko desu ka?) — each targets a different kind of unknown.
A business card exchanged when meeting someone professionally for the first time, often alongside はじめまして (hajimemashite) and よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu).
The general word for 'name'; it's what you give right after はじめまして (hajimemashite), as in はじめまして。ライアンです。(hajimemashite. Raian desu.), and what's printed on a めいし (meishi, business card).
